transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-05-28
- Start: 15:00 PDT (UTC-7)
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Elena (Redwood SE), Priya (Cascade CTO), Markus (Eng Mgr), Leah (Data Eng)

Summary:
Quick sync to review pilot economics metrics from the last run, validate caching savings, iterate on batching configs, and agree next steps for a longer throughput run and security artifacts for Private deployment evaluation.

Topics:
- Tokens / $ and tokens/sec metrics observed
- Caching (prefix + KV) savings vs hit-rate assumptions
- Batching windows and latency tradeoffs for product SLAs
- Dedicated vs hosted options for deterministic throughput
- Security checklist (SOC2, KMS, network) and next artifact handoff

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then we wanna jump into the numbers from the last 72-hour pilot. Elena, you got the sheet open?
[00:18] Elena (SE): Yep, I do. Hi Priya, Markus, Leah. Quick note, the exported run included two model variants, m-ggml-13b-quant and m-opt-7b-q8, we had a mix to show fallback behaviour. Some of the labelings in the logs were mangled, so I cleaned what I could.
[00:45] Markus: Sounds good. We had one thing earlier where tokens-per-dollar spiked on Tuesday midday, do you see what caused that?
[01:05] Elena: Yeah, so there were a couple of cold-cache bursts and one long tail of longer prompts from a test population. That amplified per-token compute. The main thing: when KV cache hit-rate drops from ~72% to ~38% our tokens per dollar degrades roughly 2.3x in that window.
[01:28] Priya: When you say KV cache, is that the prefix caching you mentioned before? I want to be sure the app-level caching lines up with our CDN layer.
[01:40] Elena: Right, there's prefix caching—so identical prompt prefixes get served from KV which saves decode work and avoids redoing key/value lookups for earlier tokens. We also have result caching at the route level for deterministic responses. The CDN you're using shouldn't conflict as long as you keep cache keys consistent.
[02:06] Leah: Minor thing, tokenizer differences across the open models produce small token-count variance; we saw ~6% difference between the two variants for the same prompt. That affected tokens/sec/$ calculations.
[02:25] Jordan: Good call. The cost model we shared earlier normalizes by tokenization for the chosen model; we'll attach per-model normalization factors.
[02:42] Markus: Walk me through the batching tradeoff again — if we increase max batch window from 20ms to 80ms what's the expected tokens/sec/$ trade?
[02:55] Elena: So, roughly: latency SLO increase ~15–35ms on p95 if you go to 80ms batching, but tokens/sec throughput improves by ~18–30% depending on sequence length distribution. For short prompts (<64 tokens) batching helps less; for long-context requests batching gives more efficiency. There's a sweet spot in our config that we recommended in the playbook, typically 30–50ms for mixed workloads.
[03:30] Jordan: And that's taking into account continuous batching vs fixed micro-batching, correct?
[03:37] Elena: Yeah, continuous batching with dynamic flush thresholds so we don't stall for SLO-critical routes. Also we prioritize routes by latency tier so customer-facing chat gets a smaller flush window.
[03:50] Priya: On the dedicated capacity side — if we reserve GPUs, do we get better tokens/sec/$ long term than hosted? We have pretty steady traffic patterns for the pilot.
[04:05] Jordan: Generally yes — dedicated pools give you predictable throughput and quieter noisy neighbor behaviour so your observed tokens/sec/$ is more stable. But committed pricing and utilization assumptions matter: if you underutilize reserved capacity, hosted can be cheaper. Our spreadsheet has a utilization sensitivity tab.
[04:26] Leah: We saw some 'blips' in the hosted run where latency briefly doubled. Could that be fallback to a different model variant?
[04:36] Elena: Possible. We had the smart routing enabled to fall back to opt-7b when the larger model was saturated. Fallback helps availability but costs can go up if the smaller model increases token count due to tokenization differences.
[05:00] Markus: Any numbers on caching savings we can expect if we standardize prefixes across the product?
[05:10] Elena: From this run: standardizing prefixes raised hit-rate from 58% to 76% on average for the set of URLs we tested. That translated to about ~42% reduction in per-token compute for cached flows — so large savings for repeatable UX flows.
[05:30] Priya: That's promising. How long before we can see that steady-state?
[05:36] Elena: Within a week of roll-in for most customer traffic patterns, but depends on churn of unique user queries.
[05:42] Jordan: Ok, quick pause — any questions on those numbers before we go deeper into the playbook configs?
[05:50] Markus: One: how are you handling prefix eviction in KV cache to avoid memory blowup?
[05:58] Elena: LRU with size limits per namespace; we also shard keys by customer to avoid cross-tenant eviction storms. For the pilot we used a 48-hour TTL with a soft size cap.
[06:10] Leah: Were there any transcription or metric mismatches that made your analysis fuzzy?
[06:14] Elena: A few logs had missing model tags hence the earlier cleanup note; also some timestamps were in local server time vs UTC which shifted some windows but not the overall conclusions.
[06:28] Jordan: Alright — playbook section: recommended per-route configs, batching hints, cache key strategy, and a short checklist for security items if you want to test Private deployment. Elena, can you summarize the per-route defaults?
[06:42] Elena: Sure: Route A (user chat): latency tier p95 < 200ms, batching flush 25ms, prefix cache enabled, max sequence 512. Route B (document summarization): latency tier p95 < 1s, batching flush 60ms, KV cache disabled for long-tail docs, prefer quantized model variants. Route C (reranking): small prompt, high qps, batching flush 15ms, use smallest compatible model with early-exit heuristics.
[07:18] Priya: For Route A we're sensitive to any p95 > 250ms — that's our SLA in prod. Can we ensure the playbook config keeps that?
[07:27] Elena: With today's traffic profile, yes — with 25–30ms batching and a small dedicated pool we hit p95 ~180–210ms. If you run a mixed spike we recommend autoscale buffer and model fallback disabled for that route.
[07:44] Markus: You mentioned early-exit heuristics for reranking — is that experimental?
[07:49] Elena: It's a mix: partial generation scoring and classifier heuristics that can truncate heavy decode when confidence is high. Works well for rerankers and reduces tokens consumed. We have a short demo clip — I'll add it to the sheet.
[08:10] Jordan: Switching to cost math: we compute tokens/sec/$ by dividing observed token throughput by total infra cost over the window (reserved + transient). For the last 72h window token/sec/$ for the mixed-model run was 12.4k tokens/sec per $1 when we had a 66% cache hit-rate, and fell to ~5.2k tokens/sec per $1 during low hit windows.
[08:41] Leah: Just to be clear that's normalized per hour and across the whole pool right?
[08:45] Elena: Correct — normalized across pool and per model variant weighted by actual traffic share.
[08:53] Priya: Do you account for tokenization differences in that metric?
[08:57] Jordan: Yes we attach a tokenization factor by model — you'll see a column in the shared sheet.
[09:05] Markus: For the 48h run you propose, what extra telemetry do you want us to enable?
[09:10] Elena: Request-level tags for route, model, cache-hit (bool), token_count, latency_ms, and a sampling of raw prompt hashes for dedupe analysis. If possible enable the CDN cache-key header pass through so we can correlate.
[09:28] Priya: Security — we need to confirm KMS and SSO integration for Private. What are the minimal asks?
[09:36] Jordan: For Private: SAML SSO, KMS integration (bring-your-own allowed), audit logs to your SIEM via syslog or S3, encrypted at rest w/ customer-managed keys. We'll send the checklist and our compliance pack.
[09:50] Markus: Do you support HSM?
[09:53] Elena: Yes, through partner KMS/HSM integrations — we can map to your vendor, we use standard PKCS interfaces for key wrapping.
[10:02] Leah: Any gotchas if we use a hybrid where some traffic is hosted and some on Private?
[10:09] Elena: Just routing complexity — you want consistent model versions and a clear routing policy. We'll recommend a model pinning strategy so behavior is uniform.
[10:20] Jordan: Back to economics: one scenario we like to show in the playbook is 'cache-first' path for known flows + rate-limited non-cache path for novel queries. That gives great tokens/$ for chatty UX.
[10:34] Priya: Does Redwood Optimize have automatic suggestions for cache TTL and batch windows?
[10:40] Elena: The product's recommendations are experimental; we propose initial defaults and show a recommended sensitivity test. Some labels in our dashboard might read 'Red Wood Opt' in the logs — minor naming glitch in earlier builds.
[10:55] Jordan: Alright let's surface a concrete example for Cascade: if you standardize 80% of your top-50 intents to be cacheable, your tokens/$ can improve about 2.8x at steady state, holding other factors constant.
[11:12] Markus: What about burst pricing on hosted when traffic spikes? Is it automatic or do you throttle?
[11:19] Elena: You can configure burst policies: allow some on-demand scale with higher unit cost, or hard-throttle to bound cost. For pilots we usually enable a soft cap then notify.
[11:33] Priya: For our executive update next week we need a simple one-pager: current tokens/$, projected steady-state tokens/$ with cache, recommended capacity path (hosted -> dedicated) and timeline.
[11:44] Jordan: We'll produce that. Elena will run the longer throughput test and I'll prepare the executive one-pager.
[11:52] Leah: Quick question about model quantization — you recommended q4_0 for the 13b? Any quality regressions?
[11:59] Elena: Small tradeoffs on rare tokens, but for most of your prompts we saw negligible quality delta using eval-set A. We included a quality guard in the playbook to monitor regressions tied to prompt sets.
[12:12] Markus: How do we instrument quality regressions to tie back to a rollout?
[12:17] Elena: We tie evals to release tags and set regression alerts: if a metric moves beyond threshold we'll auto-fallback to previous model version for that route.
[12:30] Priya: Fine. For the 48h run — do we need to do anything special with our traffic to simulate realistic mix?
[12:36] Elena: Best to run with your real traffic and add a small synthetic tail for corner-cases. We'll provide a seed script for that.
[12:45] Jordan: Ok, let's go into a few of the noisy log examples you all saw — Leah, can you share the one from May 20th?
[12:52] Leah: Yup I posted it in the shared channel — but quick summary: a small batch of long transcripts combined with a model fallback resulted in a 3x token bump for that cohort. We corrected route tagging afterwards.
[13:08] Elena: Those are the exact windows we want to watch to tune autoscale and fallback. If fallback triggers for high-cost flows we should have guardrails to route to cheaper model variants or fall back to cached best-effort.
[13:24] Markus: What's the recommended guardrail threshold? 1.5x baseline? 2x?
[13:30] Elena: We usually start with 1.7x and iterate. It's a trade between cost and availability. We'll include a recommended set in the playbook with a small config snippet.
[13:44] Jordan: Switching to telemetry and dashboards: we'll add a per-route tokens/sec/$ chart and a cache-hit heatmap. Any additional panels you want?
[13:53] Priya: Per-user heavy-hitter list so we can identify misbehaving clients.
[13:57] Leah: Also a prompt-length distribution chart so we can tune batch window by percentiles.
[14:04] Jordan: Good.
[14:06] Priya: On SOC2 artifacts — Jordan, when can we expect the compliance pack?
[14:12] Jordan: I'll send it by Monday. It includes the SOC2 attestation, data flow, and the KMS/HSM integration guide.
[14:20] Markus: Any blocker to running the 48h test?
[14:24] Elena: Just the sampling flags and the extra telemetry tags — once you flip them we'll start the run. Also let us know if you want the run to simulate higher concurrency.
[14:36] Jordan: Quick quick check — are we aligned on next steps now?
[14:39] Priya: Yes — 48h run, pricing worksheet, SOC2 docs.
[14:43] Jordan: Great. We'll recap final items and owners now.

Recap & Action Items (spoken):
[14:50] Jordan: Elena will kick off the 48h throughput run with tagged telemetry; Jordan will send the pricing and one-pager; Priya will share security contacts and network diagram. We'll sync next Tuesday for results.

Closing (informal):
[15:00] Markus: Thanks all. Looking forward to the numbers.
[15:03] Leah: Thanks, talk soon.
[15:06] Jordan: Thanks everyone, bye.

Notes on transcription quality: medium — a few speaker mislabels and timestamps mixed local/UTC. Some product names transcribed slightly off (eg 'Red Wood Opt' for Redwood Optimize).
